documents.title: Maritime Gallery Opens at Harlow Museum
documents.text:
Harlow Museum will open its long-awaited Maritime Gallery on 4 March, following a two-year renovation of the building's east wing. The centrepiece of the new gallery is a full-size reconstruction of a fourteenth-century cargo ship, assembled from timbers recovered from the harbour during the construction of a new pier. Visitors will be able to walk through the hull and handle replicas of the tools used by the shipwrights.

The museum is especially keen to attract school parties. Admission for school groups is 8 euros per student. Teachers and other accompanying adults pay 12 euros each, although one adult is admitted free for every ten students. A guided tour, which lasts 45 minutes, can be added for a flat fee of 45 euros per group, and a hands-on workshop for 3 euros per student. Groups that book at least 30 days in advance receive a 10 percent reduction on admission charges only; tours and workshops are not discounted.

Director Elena Marsh said that the gallery would be "a place where history can be touched, not just observed".

documents.title: Python for Data Analysis
documents.text:
DATA SKILLS ACADEMY | Python for Data Analysis

An eight-week online course for beginners. No prior programming experience is required, although familiarity with spreadsheets is recommended. Plan for about five hours of study a week, with a weekly live question-and-answer session with a mentor.

Fee: 59 euros per month, billed monthly. Most learners finish in two months. You may cancel at any time, and no further charges will apply.

Certificate: learners who complete all eight modules and the final project may request a certificate of completion for an additional fee of 25 euros.

Support: learners receive e-mail help within one working day, and a private community forum is open at all hours.

Refunds: if you are not satisfied, you may request a refund within 14 days of your first payment, provided that you have completed less than a quarter of the course content.

Course modules: spreadsheets and data cleaning; functions and loops; working with tables; visualisation; statistics basics; case studies; final project.

documents.title: Not for true beginners
documents.text:
Two stars out of five

I signed up three weeks ago, lured by the promise that no programming experience was needed. The first module, on spreadsheets, was easy, but the second module, on functions and loops, assumed that I already knew the basics of coding. I spent nearer twelve hours a week than five, and the live sessions were mostly attended by people who had clearly programmed before. When I asked for a refund on the twentieth day, I was told that the period for requests had passed, even though I had completed barely one module in a half. I am cancelling, but I have already paid 59 euros for the first month and I expect to be charged for the second. On the positive side, the mentor who ran the weekly session was patient and generous with her time, and the downloadable notes are excellent. The content is well made, but the course should be honest about its level.

choices: The request came after the 14-day period
The reviewer had finished more than a quarter of the course
The reviewer had not paid the monthly fee
The reviewer had already requested a certificate
questions.explanation: The refund must be requested within 14 days of the first payment; the reviewer asked on the twentieth day.

documents.title: Metroline Line 4: Engineering Works
documents.text:
METROLINE LINE 4: ENGINEERING WORKS

On Saturday 8 March and Saturday 15 March, no trains will run between Parkside and Eastfield after 20:00. Replacement buses will leave from the Parkside bus stop at 10, 30 and 50 minutes past every hour. The bus journey takes 50 minutes, compared with 25 minutes by train. Tickets remain valid on replacement buses. Passengers who need step-free access can request an accessible bus by calling the helpline at least two hours before travel.

As an alternative, passengers may take Line 2 from Parkside to Central and change there to Line 6, which will continue to run to Eastfield. This route takes about 65 minutes, including the change at Central. We apologise for any inconvenience and thank passengers for their patience while we upgrade the signalling system.

documents.title: Four-Day Week Trial Reports Strong Results
documents.text:
A six-month trial of a four-day working week involving 61 companies and about 2,900 employees has ended with 56 of the companies choosing to continue the arrangement, researchers announced on Tuesday. Participating firms, which ranged from a software developer to a fish-and-chip shop, kept pay unchanged while reducing weekly working time to around 32 hours.

On average, revenue rose by 1.4 percent during the trial, sick days fell by around two-thirds, and the number of staff resigning dropped by more than half. Managers reported that employees were more focused, and several firms said that they had cut meetings in order to protect productivity.

The results were not uniformly positive. Companies in customer service and retail found it harder to maintain continuous coverage and had to introduce rotas under which staff took different days off. Some employees reported that the compressed week left them more tired on the days that they worked. The lead researcher, Professor Ingrid Vale, cautioned that the participants had volunteered and might not represent the wider economy.

documents.title: Four-day week pilot
documents.text:
To: All employees
From: Chief Executive, Altamira Services
Subject: Four-day week pilot

Following recent research into shorter working weeks, we will begin a six-month pilot on 5 May. Office employees will work from Monday to Thursday, for 32 hours a week, on full pay. Helpline staff will work a rota so that the line stays open from 8:00 to 18:00, Monday to Friday, with each person taking one weekday off. Managers will measure results against our existing productivity targets. If targets are missed by more than 5 percent in two consecutive months, the pilot will be paused and reviewed. We will report the outcome to all staff in November. Employees who would prefer to keep a five-day pattern, for example because of childcare arrangements, may discuss alternatives with their manager. Part-time staff will have their hours reduced in proportion only if they request it.

questions.prompt: What do the results of the trial suggest?
choices: Employees are unable to work effectively on four days
Only technology firms can run a shorter week successfully
Most participants returned to a five-day week
Shorter weeks did not harm output and benefited staff
questions.explanation: Revenue rose, sick days fell, resignations dropped, and 56 of the 61 firms continued.

questions.prompt: Why does the article mention retail and customer service?
choices: To prove that sales rose in every sector
To explain why research costs are high
To show a problem facing some businesses
To name companies that left the trial
questions.explanation: These sectors found it harder to maintain continuous coverage and had to introduce rotas, a limit on the benefits.

questions.prompt: In what way does Altamira's helpline arrangement reflect the article?
choices: It uses a rota like some service firms do
It forces employees to work longer hours per day
It will close the helpline for one day a week
It avoids the need to measure productivity
questions.explanation: The article says that customer-service firms introduced rotas under which staff took different days off; Altamira's helpline staff each take one weekday off while the line stays open.

questions.explanation: The professor warned that the participants might not represent the wider economy.

questions.prompt: When would Altamira's pilot be paused?
choices: If more than five employees resign within one month
If targets are missed by 5 percent in one month
If targets are missed twice by over 5 percent
If revenue falls in each of six consecutive months
questions.explanation: The memo says the pilot will be paused if targets are 'missed by more than 5 percent in two consecutive months'.

documents.title: Call for Papers: Urban Futures Conference
documents.text:
URBAN FUTURES CONFERENCE | Call for Papers

The fifth Urban Futures Conference will be held from 2 to 4 October in Gdansk. We invite researchers and practitioners to submit proposals on the following themes: transport and mobility, housing affordability, urban green space, and the governance of smart cities.

Submission guidelines: Abstracts must not exceed 250 words and must be submitted online by 15 April. Authors will be notified of the outcome by 30 May. Accepted authors must register by 15 July; the registration fee is 280 euros for academics and 420 euros for other participants, with a 25 percent reduction for those registering before 1 June.

Accommodation: a block of rooms has been reserved at the Hotel Baltica at 95 euros per night; the offer is valid until 31 July. The conference dinner on 3 October is included in the registration fee, and a field trip to the harbour redevelopment area is planned for the afternoon of 4 October at no extra cost.

Presentations are 20 minutes long, followed by 10 minutes for questions. Each author may submit two proposals at most. Papers presented at the conference will be considered for publication in a special issue of the Journal of Urban Studies.

documents.text:
To: conference@urbanfutures.example
From: Dr. Samuel Teague
Subject: Submission query

Dear organisers,

I am a researcher at a university and would like to submit an abstract on cycling infrastructure in mid-sized cities. I have two questions. First, my abstract currently runs to 310 words; may I submit it as it stands, together with a longer supporting document? Second, I shall be travelling in the second half of April and might miss the deadline by a few days. Could you tell me whether an extension is possible? I should also like to confirm what I would pay if my proposal were accepted and I registered in May.

Best wishes,
Samuel Teague
